# Warehouse Automation & Workforce-Transition Roadmap
## Automating Five Sites Without Losing the Workforce, the Key Accounts, or the Town

*Executable plan with working tools: automation tiers, site-scoring model, attrition math, vendor contract mechanics, parallel-run standards, a benefits ledger, a tripwire protocol, communication skeletons, and a one-glance master timeline. Bracketed figures are placeholders to be set from your model — the relationships between them are the plan. The competitor's national-news failure was not bad luck; it was a design choice. This roadmap is built from its autopsy.*

---

## 1. Strategic Frame

**Situation:** Five regional warehouses, rising labor costs, 35% picker turnover, and error rates that are now costing key accounts. Vendors promise 3-year payback. Capital exists but is finite. The workforce is long-tenured, one site anchors its town's economy, and the industry just watched a competitor's rollout collapse publicly.

**Strategic reality:** Three things are simultaneously true, and the plan must hold all three:

1. **The payback is real but slower than the vendor says.** Vendor math assumes day-one full savings, 100% uptime, and zero integration cost. Honest math pays back in [4–5] years. It is still worth doing — labor inflation and error-driven account churn compound against doing nothing — but a program sized to the vendor's slide deck will be declared a failure while succeeding.
2. **35% turnover is not the problem; it is the mechanism.** At 35% annual attrition, a site sheds a third of its picking headcount every year *voluntarily*. Sequenced correctly, the workforce reduction happens through people quitting jobs they were going to quit anyway — and layoffs become the exception, not the headline.
3. **The binding constraint is not capital. It is absorption capacity** — how much change one organization's management, maintenance bench, and local trust can digest per quarter. That constraint, not the budget, sets the sequence.

**Transition arc:** [2] quarters to instrument baselines and deploy low-cost automation everywhere → pilot go-live ~quarter [4] → ramp valley quarters [5–6] → stage-gated conversions quarters [7–16], staggered ≥[1] quarter apart → company-town site converts with written commitments ~quarter [12] → steady state and full benefits realization year [3–4].

**Operating principles:**

1. **Attrition first, layoffs last.** Freeze backfills at converting sites [3] quarters before go-live. Never announce a reduction the attrition curve could have delivered.
2. **Automate the process before the people.** Software, slotting, and pick-path optimization at all five sites first — cheap, fast, zero displacement, and it builds the data baseline every later decision depends on.
3. **One site proves the model before the network funds it.** Capital releases in stage gates tied to measured results, not vendor projections.
4. **Parallel-run everything.** Big-bang cutover is a design choice, and it is the wrong one. Manual capacity stays until automation *earns* retirement of the fallback.
5. **Publish the ramp valley.** Throughput dips [10–20]% for [8–12] weeks after every go-live. If the board, the workforce, and key accounts learn this from the plan, it's a J-curve; if they learn it from experience, it's a crisis.
6. **The town is a stakeholder, not a PR problem.** Engage the mayor and the workforce before the announcement, with commitments in writing. People forgive a plan; they do not forgive a surprise.
7. **Share the gains.** A workforce that sees automation as a pay cut will sabotage it quietly and accurately. Gainsharing converts skeptics into operators.

---

## 2. The Autopsy — Design Rules from the Competitor's Failure

| What they did | Why it failed | Our rule |
|---|---|---|
| Big-bang conversion of the flagship site | One failure mode took down the whole building | Zone-by-zone cutover; manual fallback retained until automation sustains spec for [4] consecutive weeks |
| Converted into peak season | Ramp valley collided with maximum volume | Hard freeze on cutovers [Oct 15 – Jan 5]; go-lives land in demand troughs |
| Announced mass layoffs at go-live | Lost the experienced workforce exactly when the immature system needed human cover — and made national news | Attrition-first sequencing; reduction math published internally [6] months ahead; severance reserved but unneeded in the base case |
| Took the vendor's payback at face value | Board declared failure at month 18 of a real 4-year payback | Internal case ([4–5] yrs) is the published case; vendor case is a marketing document |
| Treated the workforce as cost to eliminate | Tribal knowledge walked out; errors spiked; local press turned hostile | Tenured core retrained into the higher-skill roles automation creates; gainsharing on verified savings |
| No tripwires | Small failures cascaded for weeks before anyone acted | Pre-agreed thresholds with pre-agreed responses (Section 7) |

---

## 3. Degree of Automation — Depth and Speed Are One Dial

### Automation tiers

| Level | Contents | Capex/site | Typical payback | Headcount impact | Execution risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — Process/software** | WMS upgrade, slotting optimization, pick-by-voice/RF, labor management | [$] | [<12] months | None; +[10–15]% productivity | Low |
| **2 — Mechanized assist** | Conveyors, put walls, pick-to-light, cartonization | [$$] | [18–30] months | [10–20]% of hours | Moderate |
| **3 — Goods-to-person robotics** | AMRs or shuttle/AS-RS, automated induction | [$$$] | [3.5–5] years honest case | [35–50]% of picking hours | High |
| **4 — Full automation** | AS/RS + robotic picking/packing, minimal touch | [$$$$] | [6+] years | [60+]% | Highest — reserve for greenfield |

### Program scenarios

| Scenario | Scope & pace | Peak service risk | Layoff risk | Capital peak | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Aggressive** | Level 3–4 at all five sites in [24] months | **Highest — the competitor's path** | Attrition cannot absorb the pace; forced reductions certain | [$$$$] | Rejected |
| **B — Base (recommended)** | Level 1 everywhere now; Level 3 at [3] sites sequenced over [30–36] months; Level 2 at the rest | Managed via parallel runs | Near-zero if sequencing holds | [$$$] | **Adopted** |
| **C — Slow** | Pilot + one site, then wait-and-see | Lowest | Lowest | [$] | Rejected — labor inflation and key-account erosion compound; drift risk |

**Held constant across scenarios:** technology tier per site, vendor shortlist, workforce terms, and acceptance standards. Only pace and count of Level-3 sites move. A scenario that changes two variables at once compares programs, not speeds.

**Why not C:** error rates are damaging key accounts *now*, and 35% turnover means you are already paying re-hiring and retraining costs continuously — the standing still option is not free, it is just unitemized.

**The most dangerous moment is weeks [4–12] after each go-live:** throughput is down, errors are up, the skeptics are loudest, and — post-competitor — the local press is watching. This is when companies rip out robots at the exact bottom of the J-curve. The antidote is pre-commitment: the ramp valley is named in the published plan, and the response to it is written in advance (Section 7).

**Financing note:** consider robots-as-a-service (RaaS) for the smaller sites and seasonal flex — it converts capex to opex, keeps the capital peak inside the envelope, and makes capacity reversible if a site's volume thesis changes.

---

## 4. Site-by-Site Sequence

### Scoring model (weighted)

| Criterion | Weight | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Labor cost exposure (wages × hours × turnover cost) | [25]% | Where savings are largest |
| Error-rate pain / key-account exposure | [20]% | Where quality buys revenue retention |
| Building suitability (clear height, floor flatness, power, layout) | [20]% | Retrofit cost and risk |
| Turnover rate | [15]% | Attrition's absorptive capacity — high turnover *speeds* conversion |
| Community & reputational sensitivity | [10]% | Where the sequence must slow down |
| Lease length / growth outlook | [10]% | Don't bolt fixed automation into a site you may exit; AMRs relocate, AS/RS doesn't |

### Resulting sequence (placeholder assignments — set from scoring)

| Order | Site | Level | Go-live | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (pilot) | **[C]** — mid-volume, highest turnover [45%], newest building | 3 | Q[4] | Attrition absorbs displacement; modern building de-risks retrofit; big enough to prove the model, small enough to survive its mistakes |
| 2 | **[E]** — high volume, high error pain | 3 | Q[7] | Largest quality payoff; key-account relief lands early |
| 3 | **[B]** | 3 | Q[10] | Same integration team carries compounding lessons |
| 4 | **[A]** — largest, company town | 2 + partial 3 | Q[12–14] | Converted with the town covenant (Section 5); sequenced late so the playbook is proven before the most visible site |
| 5 | **[D]** — smallest / shortest lease | 2 only | Q[15] | Level 3 economics don't clear at this scale; RaaS if volume grows |

**Sequencing rules:** stagger go-lives by ≥[1] quarter so the *same* implementation team moves site to site — learning compounds and no site gets the B-team. Never run two cutovers in the same quarter. No go-live within [90] days of peak.

---

## 5. Workforce Transition — Attrition Is the Mechanism

### The attrition math (worked example — pilot site)

- Site [C]: [180] pickers × 35% turnover = ~[63] voluntary exits per year.
- Selective backfill freeze starting [3] quarters pre-go-live: headcount drifts down [45–55] by go-live with **zero layoffs** (freeze is selective — service-critical roles still backfill).
- Automation target: −[40]% picking hours ≈ [70] roles over [24] months post-go-live.
- Residual gap after attrition: [10–20] roles → absorbed by redeployment into packing, returns, inventory, and volume growth the accuracy improvement wins back.
- **Base-case forced layoffs: zero.** Reserve severance budget anyway — honesty and insurance in one line item.

**Critical caveat:** turnover is not uniform. [60–70]% of exits happen in the first [90] days of employment. Attrition shrinks the revolving-door tail; the tenured core stays. That is the point — they are exactly who you retrain.
